See Chevron’s Analyst Ratings Chevron’s free cash flow ran between about $1 billion and $8 billion a quarter from late 2023 through 2025. Then it swung from negative in the first quarter of 2026 to $18.1 billion in the second: Part of that was cash that got tied up in the first quarter and came back in the second. Chevron’s adjusted free cash flow, which leaves out those working-capital swings, was $15.4 billion. That’s still more than three times the $4.9 billion it made a year earlier. Analysts want more. Their consensus has Chevron generating $42.9 billion of free cash flow in 2026. It made $16.6 billion in the first half, so the second half needs about $26 billion, or roughly $13 billion a quarter. That’s more than double last year’s third quarter. Oil did its part. Crude prices and refining margins rose through the third quarter, according to the EIA, and Brent averaged $114 in September, up from $104 across Chevron’s second quarter. Volumes may slip, though. Management guided to 150,000 to 200,000 barrels of oil equivalent a day of downtime in the third quarter. That follows second-quarter output of 4.07 million barrels a day, up 20% from a year earlier with Hess in the mix. Spending didn’t chase the windfall. Chevron’s capex held between $3.7 billion and $5.3 billion a quarter over the last three years: Management guided to $18 billion to $19 billion of capex for 2026, and the first half took $8.6 billion. So the second half runs a little heavier, but nowhere near enough to soak up the spike. So the second quarter’s cash went to the balance sheet. Chevron cut its debt by a record $8.4 billion. Meanwhile, the cash it spent on buybacks rose to $3.1 billion from $2.7 billion a year earlier. That was overdue. In 2025, with Brent at $69, dividends and buybacks took $24.9 billion against $16.6 billion of free cash flow, and debt covered the gap. By June 30, net debt was down to 0.6x operating cash flow, from 1.0x at the end of 2025. And the Hess Midstream exit takes about $3.7 billion more debt off the books when it closes, which Chevron expects by year-end. At its record high, Chevron trades at 12x forward earnings. That’s below its five-year average of 14x: But those forward earnings carry war-level oil prices. In the past year, analysts raised their 2026 EPS estimate 91%, to $17.51. They left 2028’s at $13.08, about where it was a year ago. That’s a 25% drop from 2026 to 2028, so the stock is priced well above 12x the earnings analysts expect to last. Chevron has guided to buybacks of $2.5 billion to $3 billion a quarter this year. With most of the debt work done, Friday’s report has to show the cash moving past that range to shareholders, or a plan to get it there. My take: with oil where it was in the quarter, the cash is the easy part. At 12x earnings that analysts expect to shrink, I’d want to see a bigger buyback before paying a record price for the stock. Of course, if the conflict with Iran eases and oil falls, Chevron’s fourth-quarter outlook could matter more than anything in Friday’s numbers. title: Exxon (XOM) and Chevron (CVX) cancel plans for their executives to travel to the UAE’s ADIPEC oil conference next week on security grounds, according to reports, citing sources - Newsquawk
content: Exxon (XOM) and Chevron (CVX) cancel plans for their executives to travel to the UAE’s ADIPEC oil conference next week on security grounds, according to reports, citing sources. Cancellations of this kind are a standard tell when corporate security teams assess elevated regional risk: major oil companies pulled executives and staff travel to Gulf events during past episodes of US-Iran tension, tanker incidents, and threats to regional energy infrastructure, typically well before any disruption materialised. The signal lies in who is acting rather than what is said publicly: in-house risk assessments at the supermajors are conservative by design, and a withdrawal on security grounds implies a live threat picture rather than diplomatic atmospherics. The relevant mechanism for crude is the risk premium channel, with past episodes of this type tending to firm prompt spreads and raise the cost of freight and insurance for Gulf loadings even where physical flows were uninterrupted. The distinction that matters is whether the concern is a general regional posture, in which case the premium fades as headlines do, or whether it precedes an actual incident, in which case the market reprices around specific chokepoints and export terminals. Worth watching are parallel cancellations by other firms or governments, official travel advisories for the region, and any guidance from the companies themselves, since a lone cancellation reads differently from a coordinated pullback. title: Chevron (CVX) is back to searching for oil and gas in far-flung places, WSJ reports - Newsquawk
content: Chevron (CVX) is back to searching for oil and gas in far-flung places, WSJ reports. A major returning to frontier exploration marks a shift in the capital allocation posture that has defined the large integrateds for most of the past cycle, when discipline, buybacks and short-cycle shale were preferred over long-lead wildcatting. Historically, this kind of pivot back toward high-impact exploration has tended to follow periods of reserve depletion and underinvestment, with companies moving once the cost of replacing barrels through acquisition exceeds the perceived risk of the drillbit. The distinction that matters is between genuine frontier commitments with material capital at risk and low-cost optionality such as seismic, licensing rounds and farm-ins; the former reprices long-dated production expectations, the latter rarely does. For the supermajor peer set, exploration news of this kind has typically been read against the backdrop of declining discovered volumes and the ageing of legacy basins, and peers have tended to move together when the strategy shift is industry-wide rather than idiosyncratic. What is worth tracking next is which basins are named, the capital commitments attached, and whether other integrateds signal similar appetite at upcoming strategy updates. title: Exxon Mobil and Chevron head into Q3 earnings boosted by crude rally, Iran conflict - TradingView
content: Exxon Mobil XOM and Chevron CVX are set to report third-quarter earnings on Friday, with analysts expecting strong year-over-year growth in earnings and revenue. Exxon Mobil is forecast to post earnings per share of $4.03, up 114.4%, and revenue of $106.02 billion, up 24.3%. Chevron CVX, on the other hand, is expected to report EPS of $4.83, up 161.1%, and revenue of $61.65 billion, up 24.0%, before market open on October 30. The oil giants head into Q3 earnings with elevated crude prices and strong refining conditions supporting expectations for another potential earnings beat. For Exxon, Permian production growth, Guyana's additional offshore capacity, and LNG expansion could help offset lower commodity prices over the coming years, SA investing group leader Daniel Sereda said. While another analyst notes that ExxonMobil is arguably the best-run integrated major, particularly in the vertical integration of its downstream and chemical segments. "In addition to the Iran conflict, Exxon has major execution risk in the Permian Basin, while its downstream performance lagged significantly in 2Q26," the analyst said, rating Exxon as a "sale because its normalized PE ratio is now 29x, which should be reserved for AI companies and not suitable for integrated oil majors." Looking at Chevron, investing group leader Luca Socci said the company is operating at peak performance, but current valuation assumes Brent remains at elevated levels indefinitely. "Once Chevron reports, the other aspect that will matter is the Q4 forecast for buybacks. If Chevron holds it below $3B, it could be a signal that Chevron's management is aware that the stock price could be too high." Separately, what remains in focus is that Chevron CVX is said to be exploring the sale of some of its older oil and gas assets in the U.S. Gulf, as it seeks to focus on newer projects and high-growth opportunities in the region. President Donald Trump has  criticized Exxon Mobil and Chevron for making “too much money” amid rising crude oil prices driven by the Iran war, with investors looking for management’s comments on the impact of the conflict and the outlook for oil prices. title: Chevron Is Up Nearly 57% in 2026. Is Its Dividend Safer Than ConocoPhillips’? - 24/7 Wall St.
content: Brent crude near $104 a barrel makes both Chevron and ConocoPhillips look like income machines right now, but one of them slashed its dividend 66% the last time oil turned ugly, and retirees cannot afford to guess which. Chevron (NYSE:CVX | CVX Price Prediction) or ConocoPhillips (NYSE:COP): which oil dividend holds up better for investors focused on retirement? Brent crude averaged roughly $104/BBL in Q2 2026, so both companies are paying out a lot of cash. Chevron shares have risen 56.79% year to date to $232.51. For retirees, the real question is which payout lasts when crude falls. These Dividend Paying Energy Superstars Are Ready To Rock Chevron is an integrated major. It pumps oil (upstream), refines it into fuel (downstream) and makes chemicals, with its U.S. refineries running at 97% utilization. When crude gets cheaper, refining can take part of the hit because its raw material costs less, whereas ConocoPhillips is a pure exploration and production (E&P) company. It sells what it pulls from the ground, so its revenue tracks commodity prices almost one for one. Its realized price of $62.33/BOE rose 36% year over year, and that same leverage works in reverse. Free cash flow is the cash left after a company funds its operations and capital spending. That cash is what really pays the dividend. In full-year 2025, Chevron produced $16.6B of free cash flow against $12.751B in dividends, covering the payout about 1.3x. ConocoPhillips generated $19.796B of operating cash flow and spent $12.553B on capital expenditures. The remainder covered its $3.995B dividend roughly 1.8x. At second-quarter 2026 prices, both payouts look secure: Chevron covered its dividend about 5.2x and ConocoPhillips about 4.3x. The full-year view favors ConocoPhillips, which also raised its base dividend 8% in Nov 2025, double Chevron’s 4% raise. Winner: ConocoPhillips. Chevron has raised its dividend for 39 consecutive years. In 2020, operating cash flow dropped to $10.6B, and the company posted a net loss of $5.6B. It still paid $9.7B in dividends and held the quarterly rate at $1.29. During the 2015 to 2016 slump, it kept the dividend at $1.07 and then edged up to $1.08. ConocoPhillips went the other way. Its quarterly dividend fell from $0.74 in 2015 to $0.25 in 2016, a 66% cut. Since then, its record has included one-off extra payments, such as $1.40 in 2022, that rise and fall with the oil cycle. A retiree can’t budget around that. Winner: Chevron. Chevron finished the second quarter with $37.075B of total debt against $189.883B of shareholder equity, a debt-to-equity ratio of 0.22. Its net debt is 0.94 times EBITDA, and it cut total debt by $8.4B in Q2 2026 alone. ConocoPhillips carries $23.29B of debt against $65.349B of equity, about 0.36. That is a solid number, but it is higher leverage, and it sits on a business with no refining buffer. Winner: Chevron. Chevron wins for anyone living on its dividends. The annualized forward payout of $7.12 works out to about a 3.1% yield at today’s price. That income comes with solid backing. The integrated model, lower leverage, and a record of holding the dividend through two oil crashes back it up. Its thinner full-year coverage matters less than it looks. Chevron spent $12.1B on buybacks in 2025, and it can trim those before it ever touches the dividend. ConocoPhillips suits investors still years from retirement who want faster dividend growth and can live with a payout tied to crude. It projects $7B incremental free cash flow by 2029, and its Willow project in Alaska targets first oil in early 2029. Over the next few quarters, watch Chevron’s coverage if Brent cools off from second-quarter levels, though for a retiree’s income today, Chevron is the stock that has already proven its payout through downturns. title: Could Project Kilby Unlock a Data Center Growth Path for TPL? - The Globe and Mail
content: Texas Pacific Land Corporation TPL is using Project Kilby to test whether its land and water assets can support a business line beyond traditional oilfield activity. The project gives TPL a concrete role in a large-scale power development tied to data center infrastructure. TPL shares have fallen 15.1% over the past three months, putting additional focus on whether emerging projects such as Kilby can broaden the growth story. The opportunity could expand TPL’s revenue base, but its financial contribution remains uncertain. Investors therefore have to separate the strategic potential from earnings already being produced by royalties, water services and surface-related activities. TPL entered an agreement to provide land and brackish water resources for Project Kilby in Reeves County, Texas. The company sold land for aggregate consideration of $42.5 million and secured the exclusive right to source aquifer-derived water for the power generation facility and other associated aspects of the project. The structure gives TPL more than one way to monetize the same development. Annual land payments are due through 2046, while the water arrangement could add another revenue stream if the project advances as planned. TPL’s established businesses remain closely connected to oil and gas activity, including royalties, water sales and produced-water royalties. Project Kilby shows how the company can apply its land and water position to power and digital infrastructure instead of relying only on drilling-related demand. The theme is also attracting major public companies. Chevron CorporationCVX is developing Project Kilby, while Microsoft CorporationMSFT has announced a new Pecos, TX, data center campus designed to add about two gigawatts of capacity and support growing artificial intelligence and cloud demand. TPL has expanded its data center strategy beyond Reeves County. During the first half of 2026, it acquired land in Shackelford and Jones counties as part of its data center and power generation initiatives, adding to the company’s efforts outside its legacy Permian footprint. Execution remains the key uncertainty. Management has said these developments require work across multiple counterparties and extensive diligence, and the financial contribution from data centers, power projects and water reuse remains uncertain. Investors should therefore treat the opportunity as an emerging growth path rather than an established earnings engine. TPL ended the second quarter with $248.6 million in cash and cash equivalents, no outstanding debt and an undrawn $500 million revolving credit facility. That balance-sheet position gives the company room to pursue development opportunities while retaining financial flexibility. Cash generation also remains substantial. TPL produced record second-quarter free cash flow of $155.5 million, up about 20% year over year. title: TPL Is Down 15.1% in 3 Months: Is the Sell-Off an Opportunity? - The Globe and Mail
content: Texas Pacific Land Corporation TPL shares have fallen 15.1% over the past three months, even as the company delivered better-than-expected second-quarter results. The decline has eased some valuation pressure, but it has not made the stock inexpensive. The investment case now rests on whether record royalty production and water-related growth can offset commodity exposure, shifting customer activity and a valuation that still stands above historical and industry benchmarks. Second-quarter 2026 earnings were $2.23 per share, beating the Zacks Consensus Estimate of $2.14 by 4.2%. Revenues of $246.1 million also topped the $243 million consensus mark by 1.3%. Oil and gas royalty revenues climbed 53.2% year over year to $145.6 million, supported by higher oil realizations and record royalty production of 39,700 barrels of oil equivalent per day. Produced water royalty revenues rose 20.6% to $37.1 million, while adjusted EBITDA reached a record $215.6 million with an 88% margin. TPL does not operate wells, but its earnings remain sensitive to oil and natural gas prices and to drilling decisions made by third-party operators. Because the company does not hedge its commodity exposure, weaker prices can reduce royalty income and may also curb demand for land and water services. Viper Energy VNOM provides useful industry context. Like TPL, it owns mineral and royalty interests primarily in the Permian Basin and relies on operators to develop acreage without requiring Viper to fund drilling, illustrating both the appeal and the external dependency of the royalty model. Second-quarter water sales volumes averaged 663,000 barrels per day, up 38% year over year but down 19% sequentially. Management linked the sequential decline to weak in-basin natural gas prices that shifted some development away from the Delaware Basin. Produced water royalty volumes moved the other way, reaching a record 4.9 million barrels per day, up about 15% year over year and 6% sequentially. TPL is also supplying land and brackish water resources for Chevron CorporationCVX through Project Kilby, giving its water assets another potential outlet beyond traditional oilfield demand. The sell-off has not erased TPL’s premium. The stock trades at 34.76X forward 12-month earnings, above its five-year median of 29.17X and the Zacks sub-industry multiple of 21.33X. That valuation leaves less room for operating disappointments. Continued production growth, healthy water activity and progress on newer initiatives may support the premium, but commodity weakness or softer third-party development could make the multiple harder to justify. The recent decline has not resolved the valuation question. TPL’s asset-light model, record production and water royalty growth remain positives, while commodity exposure and variable water demand limit visibility. title: If You'd Invested $10,000 in Chevron (CVX) Stock 1 Year Ago, Here's How Much You'd Have Today - The Motley Fool
content: (Spoiler: You're going to wish you'd invested in Chevron a year ago.) Let's play a what-if game. What if you'd plunked $10,000 in shares of energy giant Chevron (CVX +0.99%) a year ago... what would that stake be worth today? Well, the answer is impressive: $15,204 (as of Oct. 21). That's a whopping gain of 52%! To be even more impressed, note that the S&P 500 index of 500 of America's biggest companies would have turned your $10,000 into $11,629 over the same period. And before you look down on the S&P 500's performance, understand that it reflects a 16.3% gain, well above the long-term average annual S&P 500 gain of close to 10%. Obviously, that's not an ordinary performance for a stock, and it's due in large part to elevated oil prices. Here's Chevron's longer-term stock performance: Clearly, anyone investing in Chevron today should have more reasonable expectations for the stock. Perhaps more surprising is that even after this blowout one-year gain, the stock still seems reasonably valued to slightly overvalued, with a recent forward-looking price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio of 16.5, a bit above its five-year average of 12.7, and a price-to-sales ratio of 2.15, above its five-year average of 1.53. So it's not exactly a screaming bargain, but someone investing in it now and aiming to hold for many years or decades could do well. Anyone buying now will also enjoy Chevron's dividend, which recently yielded 3.14%. It's a growing payout, too: The total dividend for the year now is $6.98 per share, up from $5.16 in 2020 and $4.29 in 2016. Chevron has a lot going for it, such as promising investments in Venezuelan oil (despite geopolitical friction in the region) that could potentially double its oil output. It's expanding its operations elsewhere, too, and its refining capabilities give it an edge. Long-term, income-seeking investors might want to take a closer look at Chevron. title: AI Power Stocks Fell 7% to 13% in a Week While Exxon and Chevron Just Hit Record Highs. Here's Which Side I'd Rather Own. - The Motley Fool
content: Stocks like Oklo are high-risk, and the opportunity may not pan out, but Exxon and Chevron are built to survive hard times. Artificial intelligence (AI) is the hot topic on Wall Street and Main Street right now. But for those old enough to remember, the environment may be starting to feel like the dot-com bubble, which burst at the turn of the century. Companies like Oklo (OKLO -1.14%), NuScale Power (SMR +4.41%), and even Constellation Energy (CEG +2.52%) all fell around 7% from their highs over the last five days, as of this writing. Bloom Energy (BE -2.53%) is down 13% from its high in that shockingly short period. Meanwhile, ExxonMobil (XOM +0.70%) and Chevron (CVX +0.99%) are hitting all-time highs. There's risk in all of these stocks, but I'd rather own the stocks where the risks are easier to see and understand. That means Exxon and Chevron would be my pick. Here's why. The capital spending going into artificial intelligence is massive. AI is just a computer program, so it needs electricity to operate. That should lead to strong demand for power. That's the basic story behind companies like Oklo, NuScale, Bloom Energy, and Constellation Energy. Of the four, Oklo and NuScale are the most speculative. These two companies are attempting to build businesses around small modular nuclear reactors. The opportunity could be huge, but at this point both companies are losing money and haven't yet proven their technologies are financially viable. Only the most aggressive investors should be considering them. Bloom Energy and Constellation Energy have established and profitable businesses. Bloom Energy makes hydrogen fuel cells that provide off-grid power to AI data centers. Constellation Energy is an independent power producer selling power to the tech companies building out their AI operations. Bloom is the more aggressive option, as investors have priced a lot of good news into the stock. Even after a material pullback, the price-to-earnings ratio is still over 100x. Constellation Energy is probably the best positioned to weather an AI pullback, given the long-term contracts it signs, but irrational investors tend to throw the baby out with the bathwater when things turn south. If the AI bubble bursts, all of these stocks are likely to be hard hit, and the pullback over the last week is a sign of the all-or-nothing approach investors often take with new technologies. Meanwhile, the geopolitical conflict in the Middle East has pushed oil prices higher, resulting in strong rallies for Exxon and Chevron. Both energy giants are trading near all-time highs, which is something history has shown won't last. Eventually, oil prices will fall, and so will Exxon and Chevron's stock prices. But I'd still rather own an integrated energy giant over the AI power stocks above. The big reason: the energy cycle is well understood by the market and by these integrated energy giants. They will survive in relative stride if history is any guide. Exxon and Chevron are standouts in the integrated energy sector because of their long histories of annual dividend increases. Exxon's streak is up to 43 years, while Chevron's streak is at 38 years. Meanwhile, they both have extremely low debt-to-equity ratios, at 0.16x and 0.2x, respectively. When the oil market corrects, they will handle the hit to their businesses in relative stride and, likely, continue to reward shareholders with reliable dividends. It isn't clear what to expect from AI power companies, given that their stocks are being driven higher and lower by rapidly shifting investor sentiment. Some, like Oklo and NuScale, may never achieve profitability. Others, like Bloom Energy and Constellation, may not live up to investor expectations. Chevron and Exxon, on the other hand, have proven they can survive the full energy cycle and, given their strong financial positions, appear well positioned to do so again. I understand why investors are excited about Oklo, NuScale, Bloom Energy, and Constellation Energy. But I have a hard time quantifying the risk given the AI theme that is moving their stocks higher and lower. If I'm going to take on a risk, I prefer it to be one I can get my head around. The risks Exxon and Chevron face in the oil industry are fairly well defined by history. And so is their ability to deal with those risks. I'd rather own them and collect their reliable above-market yields of 2.2% and 3%, respectively. I don't know what to expect from companies that have tied their futures to a new technology whose future is still uncertain. Reuben Gregg Brewer has no position in any of the stocks mentioned.
